title: Casts: is, as and patterns
sub: How the CLR checks a type, why (long)(object)42 fails and where operators stay silent
cards/0/title: Up is free, down is checked
cards/0/body:
A cast to a base type or an interface is implicit: the compiler already knows a Manager is an Employee. Nothing happens at run time; the reference stays the same.

Going back down to a derived type takes an explicit cast in parentheses. The compiler does not know what really sits in the variable, so it inserts a check that runs at run time.

The same parentheses do different things: for numbers, (int)3.9 is a conversion of the value (you get 3); for references, it is only a check of the type, and the object does not change.
cards/1/title: How the CLR checks a cast
cards/1/body:
For (Manager)o the compiler emits the IL instruction castclass. At run time the CLR reads the type pointer from the object and compares it with Manager. No match — it walks up the parent chain, and for an interface, through the type's list of interfaces. Found — the cast succeeds. Not found — InvalidCastException.

An important detail: null passes any cast to a reference type. There is nothing to check, so there is no exception.
cards/1/deep: In modern .NET this logic lives in managed code (the CastHelpers class in the runtime) and uses a cache of cast results. A cast to a sealed class is often reduced by the JIT to a single pointer comparison: there are no subclasses, so the type must match exactly. A cast to an interface or to a class deep in a hierarchy costs more. These are nanoseconds, but in a hot loop over millions of objects the difference shows up in a profiler.
cards/2/q: Manager derives from Employee. Which line throws InvalidCastException?
cards/2/explain: o holds an Employee, not a Manager: a parent does not become a subclass. The null line passes: casting null to a reference type always succeeds.
cards/3/body:
is and as compile to the IL instruction isinst: the same check, but without an exception. is returns a bool, as returns the reference or null.

Older code often checks the type twice: first with is, then with a cast. The pattern is Manager m does one check and hands you a variable of the right type straight away.
cards/4/q: Match the expression to what happens when o is not a Manager
cards/5/q: Why does int n = o as int; not compile?
cards/5/options/0: as returns null on failure, and an int cannot be null
cards/5/options/2: An int cannot be taken out of an object
cards/5/options/3: You have to write as Int32
cards/5/explain: For value types write o as int? or, better, o is int n: the check and the unboxing in one step.
cards/6/title: is null and is not null
cards/6/body: A class can overload == — and then x == null calls its code, which may be wrong or slow. The patterns is null and is not null never call overloaded operators: the compiler compares the reference itself with null.
cards/7/body:
A boxed int is a heap object whose type pointer says "Int32". Unboxing (IL unbox) checks that the box holds exactly the requested type and copies the value. It does no numeric conversion at all.

That is why (long)(object)42 fails with InvalidCastException, even though (long)42 works. Unbox to the exact type first, then convert.
cards/7/code:
object o = 42;          // the box holds Int32
long a = (long)o;       // InvalidCastException
long b = (long)(int)o;  // unbox the int, then widen
int c = (int)(object)null!; // NullReferenceException
cards/7/deep: The "exactly the same type" rule has exceptions. An enum and its underlying integer type unbox into each other: (DayOfWeek)(object)1 works. A boxed int can be unboxed into int?, and a boxed int? does not exist at all: boxing turns a Nullable into either a box with an int or null. Unboxing null into int gives a NullReferenceException, into int? simply null.
cards/8/q: object o = 42; Which expression runs without an exception?
cards/8/explain: The box can only be unboxed into Int32. After that, (long) is an ordinary widening numeric conversion.
cards/9/title: Conversion operators are invisible through object
cards/9/body:
A user-defined explicit operator is a static method. The compiler picks it based on static types: from Celsius to Fahrenheit, it calls the operator. But if the value sits in an object, the compiler sees "object → Fahrenheit" and emits a plain unbox. At run time the box holds a Celsius, not a Fahrenheit — InvalidCastException.

The same scenario breaks code during a refactoring: a parameter changes from Celsius to object, everything compiles, and the cast starts failing.
cards/10/q: Which lines throw InvalidCastException? Select all.
cards/10/explain: A string is not an int; unboxing needs the exact type; a conversion operator is not called through object. null passes a cast to string, and an int unboxes fine from a box holding an int.
cards/11/explain: is Manager m is a type check and a variable in one step. is not null checks the reference without any overloaded !=.
